name: Antepartum Haemorrhage (Placenta Previa, Abruptio Placentae, Vasa Previa)

reference.source: Sakshi Arora Obstetrics 9th Edition / RCOG Green-top Guideline on APH
clinicalPearls: Placenta previa presents with painless, causeless, recurrent bright red vaginal bleeding in a soft non-tender uterus
Abruptio placentae presents with painful dark vaginal bleeding, uterine hypertonus, woody tenderness and fetal distress
Digital vaginal examination is strictly contraindicated in antepartum haemorrhage until placenta previa is ruled out by ultrasound
Vasa previa causes fetal exsanguination upon rupture of membranes, diagnosed by fetal bradycardia and positive Apt test
Couvelaire uterus uteroplacental apoplexy results from widespread myometrial extravasation of blood, managed conservatively
reference.pathophysiology: Antepartum haemorrhage is vaginal bleeding from twenty-four weeks gestation to fetal delivery. Placenta previa occurs when blastocyst implantation in the lower uterine segment covers or abuts the internal cervical os. Progressive thinning of the lower segment in late pregnancy shears placental attachments, causing painless maternal hemorrhage. Abruptio placentae results from rupture of maternal decidual spiral arterioles, creating a retroplacental hematoma that shears the placenta off the uterine wall, releasing thromboplastin into maternal circulation and triggering DIC.
additionalDifferentials: Local cervical lesions (polyp, ectropion, invasive carcinoma)
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound (gold standard for placental localization and internal os distance)
Coagulation profile, fibrinogen and D-dimer (for suspected abruption and DIC)

figures.alt: Diagram illustrating three causes of antepartum haemorrhage: placenta previa (placenta covering cervix), abruptio placentae (placental detachment with hematoma), and vasa previa (fetal vessels over cervix).
